title: FRM Foundations, part 3: the classic financial disasters and their shared pattern
subtitle: LTCM, the 2008 crisis and the lesson that keeps repeating: leverage, mispriced correlation, and liquidity risk all arriving at once
whyItMatters: GARP puts these case studies on the exam not so you can recite dates, but because the failure pattern repeats almost identically across decades: high leverage, correlation assumptions set during calm periods, and liquidity risk hitting exactly when capital is needed most. Recognising that pattern early is a core risk manager skill.
openingQuestion: Why did Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) collapse in 1998?
openingOptions: The fund's pricing model got a basic mathematical formula wrong
Extreme leverage plus an assumption that markets were uncorrelated
The fund was brought down by internal accounting fraud
A sudden Fed rate rise wiped out the value of its whole bond portfolio
explanation: LTCM ran more than 25 times its capital in leverage, on the basis of a model treating its arbitrage pairs as close to uncorrelated, so total risk looked low. When Russia defaulted on its bonds in 1998, completely unrelated markets suddenly moved in the same direction (correlations heading toward 1) at exactly the moment the fund needed liquidity most - the phenomenon known as correlation breakdown in a crisis.

diagram.label: High leverage multiplies risk several times over
The model assumes low correlation under normal conditions
An unexpected shock correlates every asset at once
Forced to sell for a margin call just as liquidity dries up

realWorldExample.description: Securitised subprime debt (subprime MBS and CDOs) was rated AAA on the assumption that house prices in different states were uncorrelated. When house prices fell nationwide together, that assumption collapsed at the same moment as an entire investment banking system running 30 times leverage or more. Credit risk, market risk and liquidity risk all struck simultaneously - exactly LTCM's pattern a decade earlier, only at system-wide scale.

quiz.question: What does correlation breakdown, or correlation convergence, in a crisis mean?
options: Correlation between assets holds steady whatever the market does
A crisis makes assets suddenly move in the same direction
The correlation between equities and bonds is always exactly 1
A phenomenon that only ever occurs in emerging markets
quiz.explanation: This is why a risk model built on 'normal' historical data always understates tail risk: it is precisely during a crisis - when diversification is needed most - that correlations between assets jump. Correlation is not a stable parameter, equities and bonds are frequently negatively correlated in calm periods, and the 1998 and 2008 episodes both centred on developed markets rather than emerging ones.

quiz.question: How does high leverage make a crisis worse?
options: Leverage reduces risk by spreading capital across many more positions
Leverage is an accounting matter and does not affect cash flow
Margin calls force sales at any price, causing a chain of selling
Leverage only affects returns while the market is rising
quiz.explanation: At 25 times leverage, a loss of 4% of asset value already wipes out the entire equity. Once losses hit the threshold, the lender demands additional margin - forcing an immediate sale of assets to raise cash, usually at precisely the moment prices are falling hardest, which pushes prices down further still. Spreading borrowed money across more positions does not reduce risk, and margin calls are an unmistakably cash event.

quiz.question: What do LTCM in 1998 and the 2008 financial crisis have in common?
options: Both were caused by senior bank executives falsifying the accounts to hide losses from regulators
Both combined high leverage, models understating crisis correlation, and liquidity risk at once
Both affected a single isolated investment fund and never spread out into the wider financial system
Both happened because interest rates had been held far too low for far too long a period
quiz.explanation: The pattern repeats: high leverage multiplies risk, a model built on 'normal' data understates the chance of assets correlating together in a crisis, and when the shock lands, liquidity demands (selling assets, meeting margin calls) hit across the whole system simultaneously. Neither episode turned on fraud, and both spread well beyond the institutions where they started.

quiz.question: Why were subprime mortgage securities rated so highly before 2008 despite their real risk?
options: The model assumed regional house prices were barely correlated
Because subprime lending rates were lower than prime lending rates
Because the rating agencies skipped the analysis to earn higher fees
Because the government outright guaranteed every subprime loan made
quiz.explanation: It was exactly LTCM's modelling error: an assumption of low correlation drawn from 'normal' historical conditions, since house prices had rarely fallen nationwide together before. When the systemic shock arrived, that assumption collapsed and a portfolio that looked diversified lost value all at once. Subprime rates were in fact higher, not lower, and no blanket government guarantee existed on these loans.

quiz.question: What pattern shows up in nearly every major financial disaster?
options: Organised fraud reaching the most senior levels of management
High leverage resting on an assumption that risk is diversified
Regulators lacking the authority to intervene in time
The sudden collapse of a market that nobody had forecast
quiz.explanation: The same machine runs again and again: the model says risk is low because correlation is low, so more is borrowed to amplify a thin return, and then the crisis pulls every correlation toward one. Leverage turns a survivable loss into a default. Fraud features in some episodes but is not the common thread, and these collapses were generally forecast by somebody - the warnings were simply not acted on.

keyTakeaways: The pattern repeats across disasters: high leverage + a model understating crisis correlation + liquidity risk arriving at once
Correlation breakdown in a crisis: assets that looked unrelated move together exactly when diversification is needed most
Leverage amplifies gains and losses alike, and margin calls force selling just as prices fall hardest, creating a downward spiral
LTCM (1998) and the 2008 crisis follow the same failure pattern, differing only in scale - from one fund to the whole banking system

practicePrompt.question: A fund reports a 'well diversified' portfolio on the basis of low historical correlations across the last 5 stable market years. Which risk should you question straight away?
options: Currency risk, since the fund may invest overseas
Whether those correlations converge in a market crisis
Tax risk, since each asset may face a different tax rate
The risk that the management fee is simply too high
practicePrompt.explanation: Correlation measured over a calm period is almost always lower than correlation actually realised in a crisis. This is the modelling error that led LTCM, and the CDOs of the pre-2008 era, to misjudge how diversified their portfolios really were.

summary.keyIdea: The disasters differ in scale and match in pattern: high leverage, models understating correlation, and liquidity vanishing exactly when you have to sell.
summary.commonMistake: Reading each episode as a separate story. What is worth learning is not the detail of LTCM or of 2008 but the three elements that repeat in both.

application.title: Apply the pattern to your own portfolio
application.message: For any position, ask three questions: how much leverage is behind it, are the assets genuinely independent, and how long would it take to sell if selling became urgent.
application.secondary: Those three questions are the whole pattern, rewritten in a form you can use.

sections.text: GARP does not put historical case studies on the exam to test your memory for dates. The purpose is for candidates to recognise that although financial instruments change with each decade, the pattern leading to collapse barely changes at all.
The three components that repeat in every major disaster

sections.title: The shared pattern
sections.subtitle: Present in both LTCM in 1998 and the 2008 crisis, differing only in scale

concepts.def: Amplifies gains and losses alike; even a relatively small shock is enough to wipe out the equity and trigger a margin call.
A model built on data from calm periods reports low correlation, but a crisis makes assets suddenly move in the same direction.
When everyone has to sell to repay debt or meet margin calls, they all sell at once, driving prices lower and draining liquidity exactly when it is needed most.

sections.label: Why a mathematically correct model still fails
sections.text: LTCM's model had no calculation error - the formulas were correct given the inputs. The problem was that the inputs (low correlations, estimated from normal historical data) stopped being true under extreme conditions. This is why a risk manager always has to ask: what does this model assume, and does that assumption still hold when everything goes wrong at the same time?

lines: Three questions to ask every time: where is the leverage, will the assumed correlation hold in a crisis, and who will need to sell at the same moment I do.
The Foundations stage ends here; the Operational Resilience and Liquidity Risk stages that follow go deeper into each specific risk type.
